catalog_quote: [4.2.1, p.478] In Spoken Sinhala, usually the initial syllable receives the stress [7]. Example: /kə'rənəva/ - to do /am'ma/ - mother /po'tak/ - a book Even the words can have more than one stress per word. In words of long vowels, then the stress falls even on the long vowel. Example: /ha':muduruvo':/ - monk /ma':liga':və/ - castle ... [6, p.481] Unlike in English, Sinhala does not make a very clear distinction between stressed and unstressed syllables. In Sinhala, the position of the stress is fixed in relation to the word. Sinhala words nearly always have the stress on the first syllable, irrespective of the number of syllables in the word. sweep_summary: Sinhala (sinh1246, catalog 'weight-hedged' / weight-sensitive (tentative)). this search of works with stress in the title's two title hits are one work: Letterman 1997, the Cornell dissertation on Sinhala word-internal prosody (Glottolog 174678 and its duplicate 654776, the latter auto-harvested from a Kipsigis paper's bibliography). Both already listed. It is squarely about Sinhala word stress (abstract: Ch. 5 'data on minimal word alternations, stress assignment, and vowel reduction provides evidence that the foot is fundamental'), but no open copy exists: online only via ProQuest pqdiss:9728373 (login wall), print at Cornell (Uris Oversize Thesis P30 1997 L65 +), eCommons 0 hits, CORE/OpenAIRE/archive.org/the Internet Archive empty or offline, Cornell plab (Letterman 1994 WPCPL 9) 403 under three user readers. Its rule is known only through Nash's relay held by the project ('primary stress tends to fall on the initial or peninitial syllable, whichever is heavier.. some heavy syllables carry secondary and not primary stress'), which is what the catalog hedge already encodes. Priority high: Letterman 1997 remains the single source most likely to resolve the initial-vs-heavy ranking. Extra open find: Fenger & Weisser 2025 (lingbuzz/006932, downloaded and read) mentions only schwa reduction in non-stressed open syllables citing Letterman; silent on placement. No new deciding statement; catalog's classification unchanged.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every quoted passage (Wasala & Gamage 4.2.1/6/Abstract, Geiger 1938 secs 5.1 and 6, Nash sec. 4 and the Letterman relay) is present verbatim at the stated locators in the text files we hold. Deciding source: a 2005 TTS working paper by computer scientists relaying Inman 1986 and Karunatillake, backed by a one-paragraph 1938 remark and a working-paper acoustic study of verbs; the specialist literature (Letterman 1997 dissertation on exactly this topic, Gair & Paolillo 1997, Chandralal 2010, Gair 2003) is unheld, so the best available description is not in hand. Newly downloaded Perera & Daniel Jones 1919 (pp. 13-15) gives the most explicit rule now obtained: weak, non-contrastive stress that tends to fall on the leftmost long syllable (long V, diphthong, closed, geminate), otherwise on the first (or first/second) syllable. sources.quote: '56. Stress (force-accent) is not a "significant" element of speech in Sinhalese ... 58. All stress in Sinhalese is weak ... 59. ... There are no strict rules regulating the position of the stress in words of two or more syllables. There are, however, certain tendencies ... 60. ... "long syllable" is used to denote a syllable containing either (1) a long vowel, or (2) a diphthong, or (3) a short vowel followed by two consonants, or (4) a short vowel followed by a long consonant. For the purposes of syllable length, the groups mb, nd, n̆ḍ, ňg, ňj count as single consonants. 61. Tendency No. 1.—
sources.note: Phonetician's explicit algorithm (stress the leftmost long syllable, CVV/diphthong/CVCC/geminate = long; else initial or initial~second), with examples up to the fifth syllable; ranks heavy over initial, which our record leaves unranked.

sources.citation: Fenger, Paula & Philipp Weisser. 2025. Matching domains: The syntax, morphology, and phonology of the verb in Sinhala. lingbuzz/006932 (to appear in Natural Language & Linguistic Theory). [found during this search of works with stress in the title; not in the target list]
sources.quote: One important process that needs mentioning is that short vowels in non-stressed, open syllables are frequently reduced to schwa (see Letterman 1997). The causative morpheme, for example, surfaces as /-w@-/ in (3), because it occurs in an open syllable, and all examples below, but underlyingly it is -wa- (Parawahera 1990; Letterman 1997).
sources.note: Paper is about umlaut domains and negation in the verb; stress is mentioned only in passing (vowel reduction to schwa in non-stressed open syllables, attributed to Letterman 1997). No statement of where word stress falls; a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing else on Sinhala.
